rationale: Daniel names Joakim and Chronicles names Jehoiakim in their accounts of Nebuchadnezzar's assault upon Judah's royal house. The named ruler, Babylonian attacker and Jerusalem setting connect the narratives, while their native names and regnal dates are retained.

Both accounts describe vessels from the Lord's house being carried to Babylon and placed in the Babylonian king's temple. This identifies the sacred objects' removal, not merely a general exile theme.

Isaiah warns that royal descendants will be taken into the Babylonian king's household as eunuchs; Daniel describes the selection of royal and noble Israelite youths for that court. The parallel does not establish any individual youth's descent from Hezekiah.

The king requires literate youths able to learn letters and the Chaldean language. The later account attributes the four youths' knowledge, understanding and literary skill to God, connecting the required abilities with their divine provision.

The youths are to learn letters and the Chaldean language for royal service; Moses, brought up by Pharaoh's daughter, learns Egyptian wisdom. Both passages describe an Israelite figure's education within a foreign royal setting.
The king prescribes food and a period of education before court service. The later presentation and examination of the youths enact that arrangement and report its result.
Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah are introduced together among the Judean youths; Daniel later returns to those same named companions to share the court's crisis.
The naming of Daniel as Baltasar is explicitly recalled when the king addresses Daniel, whose name is Baltasar. This concerns Daniel's court name, not the later king of that name.
The three companions receive the court names subsequently used in the accusation against the Jewish officials who refuse the image. The names link the renamed youths to the furnace narrative.
Daniel resolves to avoid the royal food and wine; the proposed vegetable-and-water trial and the subsequent replacement of those provisions show how that resolve is carried out.

God gives Daniel favor with the eunuch in a foreign household. Joseph likewise prospers through the Lord's presence and finds favor with his Egyptian master; both accounts connect divine help with favor under foreign authority.
The eunuch fears that the youths will look worse than their peers and endanger him. Their healthier appearance after the trial answers that specific concern.
Daniel proposes ten days of vegetables and water; the later examination after ten days reports the youths' better appearance. The stated trial and its measured outcome correspond.
Daniel asks that their appearance be compared with the youths eating royal provisions. The later comparison reports precisely the favorable appearance on which his proposal depends.
The youths' better appearance after ten days answers Daniel's proposal to test their diet for that period and compare their appearance with those receiving royal provisions.
The continuing substitution of vegetables for the appointed food and wine implements Daniel's earlier resolve to avoid defiling provisions and his request for an alternative diet.
God gives Daniel understanding of visions and dreams; Joseph similarly says that the explanation of dreams comes through God. Both passages locate interpretive ability in divine help.
The gift of understanding visions and dreams is exercised when the mystery is revealed to Daniel in a night vision. His thanksgiving then credits God with the wisdom and answer received.
The presentation of the youths after the appointed days returns to the king's earlier requirement that they be educated before entering his service.

The king finds none comparable to the four youths and places them in his service; the preceding account has attributed their learning and wisdom to God's gift. The same four recipients are subsequently recognized at court.

Daniel and his companions surpass the learned experts in the king's examination. The queen later recalls Daniel as wiser than Babylon's wise men and as an interpreter for Nebuchadnezzar, continuing that account of his exceptional understanding.

Daniel's continuation until Cyrus's first year meets the same royal-year setting in which Ezra records Cyrus's proclamation concerning Jerusalem. The comparison identifies the setting without adding an unreported action by Daniel.
Nebuchadnezzar's dream disturbs his sleep; Pharaoh likewise dreams and is troubled when morning comes, then seeks interpretation. Both court narratives begin with a ruler troubled by a dream.

Nebuchadnezzar summons the court's specialists over his dream, as Pharaoh summons Egypt's interpreters and wise men. Both accounts distinguish that consultation from the later divinely enabled interpretation.
The king declares his disturbance and desire to understand the dream. Pharaoh's troubled soul and unsuccessful consultation describe the corresponding difficulty in the Joseph account.

The specialists ask the king to tell the dream so that they can interpret it; they repeat that request after his demand for disclosure. The repetition makes their dependence on receiving the dream explicit.

The king threatens the specialists if they cannot disclose the dream and its interpretation. The later order to destroy Babylon's wise men turns that threat into the crisis affecting Daniel and his companions.
The king promises rewards and honor for disclosing the dream and its interpretation; Daniel later receives gifts and authority after doing so.
The renewed request that the king first tell the dream repeats the specialists' original condition for giving an interpretation, emphasizing the unresolved demand between them and the king.

The king accuses the specialists of seeking delay. Daniel also asks for time, but then calls for fasting, supplication and divine help concerning the mystery before receiving its disclosure in a night vision.

The king demands disclosure of the dream as evidence that its interpretation can be trusted; the specialists answer that no human can meet the demand and place disclosure beyond mortals. Their reply exposes the difficulty behind the threatened judgment.

relationship: same-chapter human inability and divine disclosure
rationale: The specialists deny that a human can disclose the king's matter. Daniel likewise denies that the court's experts can reveal it, but points to God in heaven as the revealer of mysteries.

The specialists say the matter exceeds human ability and refer to an angel whose dwelling is not with flesh. Daniel's answer instead directs the king to God in heaven who reveals mysteries; the two statements are compared without identifying the angel with God.

The king orders the wise men brought out, followed immediately by the death decree in 2:13. Daniel later tells Arioch not to destroy them, interrupting that process by offering disclosure of the mystery.

The death decree reaches Daniel and his companions. Daniel subsequently calls for fasting, supplication and help so that he and those with him will not perish with the other wise men, and the mystery is then revealed.

Arioch is introduced as the chief cook ordered to bring out the learned men. The later account explicitly identifies his commission to kill them, then shows him receiving Daniel's appeal and bringing the interpreter to the king.

Daniel asks why the royal decree is so severe. The earlier exchange supplies its specific background: the king insists on disclosure of the dream itself and threatens the specialists who cannot provide it.

Daniel requests time before giving the interpretation; the earlier exchange shows the king accusing the specialists of buying time. The juxtaposition contrasts Daniel's request with the delay already suspected at court.
The companions to whom Daniel reports the matter are the same Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah introduced with him among the Judean youths.

Daniel calls for fasting, supplication and help from the Lord Most High concerning the mystery and the threatened lives of himself and his companions. The revelation and his subsequent thanksgiving record the answer to his request.
Daniel receives the mystery in a night vision and blesses God; Joseph similarly says that dream explanations come through God. The connection concerns the divine origin of the answer.

Daniel blesses the Lord as the possessor of wisdom and majesty; Job assigns wisdom, power, counsel and understanding to God. Both place wisdom in God as the source of understanding, while their distinct descriptions of divine greatness are retained.

relationship: divine authority over rulers and wisdom
rationale: Daniel says God changes rulers and grants wisdom. Job describes God seating kings, overthrowing rulers and knowing the elders' understanding, joining political authority and understanding under God's power.
Daniel says God reveals deep and dark things and knows what is in darkness. Job likewise speaks of uncovering deep things from darkness and bringing death's shadow into light.

Daniel's confession that God knows what is in darkness corresponds to the psalm's declaration that darkness does not hide from God. This uses the explicit darkness and knowledge clauses, without rewriting Daniel's final dwelling phrase.

relationship: same-chapter thanksgiving for an answered request
rationale: Daniel thanks God for making known everything he requested. His earlier call for fasting, supplication and help, followed by the night revelation, identifies the request and its answer.
Daniel's command not to destroy the wise men directly interrupts the royal decree that had ordered their destruction and threatened Daniel and his companions.

Arioch now brings the Judean captive who can disclose the mystery before the king. He had first appeared as the chief cook ordered to bring out Babylon's learned men; the same official moves from enforcing the crisis to presenting its answer.
The king addresses Daniel as the one named Baltasar, explicitly recalling the court name given when the youths were renamed.
Daniel denies that the court's specialists can disclose the king's mystery. Pharaoh's interpreters and wise men likewise fail to explain his dream before Joseph is summoned.
Daniel says God has made known to the king what is to come. Joseph likewise explains that God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do, treating the royal dream as divine disclosure.

Daniel says the reclining king saw what must happen in the last days and that the Revealer disclosed the coming events. Joseph likewise says God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do, treating the royal dream as divine disclosure.
Daniel denies that the mystery was revealed because he possesses superior wisdom. Joseph similarly refuses to locate the saving answer in himself apart from God.

The impressive statue introduced in the dream becomes the subject of Daniel's announced interpretation, which identifies its successive materials with royal powers. The connection follows the account's own explanation of its image.
The statue's gold head, silver chest and arms, and bronze lower body are explained as the king and succeeding kingdoms. The explanation follows the same sequence of materials.

The iron legs and mixed iron-and-clay feet are interpreted through subduing strength and a divided, imperfectly joined kingdom. The target explains those particular materials rather than assigning unnamed nations to them.
The stone cut without hands strikes the statue's feet; Daniel later relates that stone to the kingdom God establishes and the destruction of the other kingdoms.

The shattered statue and the stone becoming a mountain that strikes the earth are explained through God's enduring kingdom bringing the other kingdoms to an end. The source's wording about striking the earth is retained.

relationship: divine grant and withdrawal of kingship
rationale: Daniel attributes Nebuchadnezzar's kingship and power to the God of heaven. The later heavenly sentence removes his kingdom and declares that God gives human kingship to whomever He wishes.

The gold head is identified with Nebuchadnezzar's extensive dominion over living creatures; the later tree vision also identifies its great, sheltering image with the king and the peoples serving him.
The succeeding kingdoms, including the bronze kingdom, interpret the silver and bronze portions of the statue already described in the dream.

The fourth kingdom is like iron that subdues everything and cuts down every tree; the later fourth beast has iron teeth and devours, pounds and tramples. The shared iron and destructive dominion are noted without supplying an empire identification.
The divided kingdom and the mixture of pottery and iron explain the statue's feet, which were described as partly iron and partly clay.
The strong and shattered portions of the kingdom explain the mixed iron-and-clay feet of the statue. The contrast follows the materials already given in the vision.
The failure of the human mixture to hold together explains the iron and clay in the statue's feet. The interpretation retains the vision's two incompatible materials.

God's kingdom will never be destroyed; the one like a son of man receives everlasting authority and a kingdom that will never be destroyed. Both visions contrast enduring dominion with the passing royal powers around them.

Daniel promises a kingdom established by God that will not be destroyed. Gabriel announces that God will give Jesus David's throne and a kingdom without end, sharing the explicit promise of enduring divine kingship.
Daniel's concluding explanation recalls the stone cut from a mountain without hands and its destruction of the statue's materials. Those are the events shown in the dream itself.

Nebuchadnezzar orders sacrifices and libations to Daniel after prostrating himself before him. At Lystra the priest and crowd likewise propose sacrifices to human messengers. Acts explicitly records the apostles' refusal; Daniel's response to the ordered honors is not reported here.

Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges Daniel's God as God of gods and Lord of kings. His later thanksgiving again uses the titles God of gods, Lord of lords and King of kings after another demonstration of divine authority.
The gifts and authority conferred on Daniel fulfill the king's earlier promise of rewards and honor for making known the dream and its interpretation.

Daniel petitions for appointments for his three companions over Babylonia's affairs. The later accusers identify those same men as Jewish officials appointed by the king, confirming the offices that the petition requested.

Nebuchadnezzar makes the image that the ensuing proclamation requires people to worship. Exodus forbids making an idol for oneself and bowing to or serving it, supplying the command opposed by this royal demand.

Royal officials are summoned to the image's dedication; officials later gather to inspect the men whom the fire has not harmed. The two assemblies frame demanded worship and public evidence of rescue.

The herald addresses nations, peoples and languages before the command to worship the image. The final decree again addresses nations, tribes and languages, but now forbids blasphemy against the God who rescued the three men.

The royal command requires bowing to a manufactured golden image. Exodus explicitly forbids bowing to or serving such images, making the conflict one of worship rather than merely disobedience to a ruler.
The furnace is announced as the penalty for refusing to bow; the king later orders the three men bound and cast into it, carrying out that specific threat.

The nations bow when the music sounds, while the accusation singles out three Jewish officials who refuse to serve the idol or bow to the image. Their refusal contrasts with the reported public compliance.

The Chaldean accusation initiates the attack on Jewish officials over their refusal to worship the image. In the later court narrative, officials devise a religious restriction to bring Daniel down because of his prayer to God.
The accusers repeat the king's command to bow to the golden image at the musical signal. The earlier proclamation supplies the specific order they invoke.
The accusers repeat the furnace penalty for refusing to bow, recalling the exact sanction already announced by the herald.

The accused men are named as the Jewish officials appointed over Babylonia. The earlier account records Daniel petitioning for those same three companions to be appointed over Babylonia's affairs; the accusation identifies them as appointed officials.

The angry king has the three named men brought before him; after their preservation he calls the same men out of the furnace as servants of the Most High God. The renewed summons marks a change in his acknowledgment of them.
The king questions their refusal to serve his gods or bow to his image. Their answer trusts the heavenly God's rescue and expressly maintains that they will not serve the idol or bow to the image.
The king asks what god can rescue them from his hands. His later confession says their God saved them through His angel and that no other god can rescue in this way.
The three men declare that their God can and will rescue them from the furnace and the king. The witnesses subsequently find them unburned, and the king acknowledges that their God saved them.

relationship: faithful adherence to a worship command
rationale: The men state that they neither serve the king's idol nor bow to it. Their stated allegiance corresponds to the command to have no other gods and not bow to or serve manufactured images.
The king orders the furnace heated sevenfold. The later description of its fueling explicitly reports the sevenfold heating, connecting the command with its execution.
The king orders the men bound hand and foot and thrown into the furnace; he later sees them walking unbound in the fire without harm. The reversal concerns the stated bonds as well as survival.
The men are thrown into the furnace still clothed. The later inspection finds unchanged trousers, unburned hair and no smell of fire, making their bodily and material preservation explicit.
The narrative repeats the sevenfold heating and the binding and casting of the men, showing that the king's preceding orders have been carried out.
The flame kills those who bound the companions, but the companions themselves are preserved. The later inspection supplies public evidence of their preservation: untouched bodies and no fire damage.

The worshippers are named Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, the Judean names of the three companions introduced with Daniel. This links the prayer to the youths known elsewhere in the episode by court names.
Azariah and his companions pray and give thanks amid the fire while their captors stoke it. Paul and Silas likewise pray and sing hymns while confined with their feet secured in stocks.
Azariah's prayer blesses the God of the fathers and His enduring name. The later communal hymn opens with that same blessing of the fathers' God and His name.
Azariah confesses that God's deeds and judgments are righteous. Daniel's later prayer likewise calls God righteous in the calamities brought upon a people who did not obey His voice.
The prayer attributes Jerusalem's judgment to the people's sins. Daniel later appeals for wrath to turn from Jerusalem while confessing that the people's sins made the city and people a reproach.
Both prayers confess collective sin, lawless conduct and departure from God's commands, placing the speakers within the people's wrongdoing rather than treating them as detached observers.
Azariah says the people failed to keep the commands given for their good; Daniel's later confession says Israel refused God's voice and abandoned the law, bringing its curse upon them.
The prayer calls the judgments brought upon the people true. Daniel's later prayer similarly says the announced calamities came according to the covenant and affirms God's righteousness in them.

Azariah describes being handed over to hostile enemies and an unjust king. Chronicles likewise describes God handing the people into Chaldean power, followed by destruction and captivity; the shared connection is the judgment of exile.

The prayer says the speakers cannot open their mouths because shame and reproach have come upon them. Daniel's later prayer similarly contrasts God's righteousness with the shame of Judah, Jerusalem, Israel and their rulers because of sin.

The prayer asks God not to hand the people over utterly or dissolve the covenant. In Leviticus God says He did not disregard them in enemy territory so as to consume them or dissolve His covenant, and that He will remember it. The petition appeals to that covenant fidelity.

Azariah appeals for the sake of Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Exodus describes God hearing Israel's groaning and remembering His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the same patriarchal covenant invoked for help.
The prayer recalls the promise of descendants like heaven's stars and the seashore's sand. Genesis records those two images together in the promise to Abraham.

The people lament their diminished numbers and low condition because of sins. Deuteronomy warns that disobedience will leave them few after being as numerous as heaven's stars, matching the prayer's contrast with the preceding promise.

relationship: shared deprivation of rule and worship
rationale: The prayer laments the lack of rulers and sacrificial worship. Hosea likewise describes Israel remaining without king, ruler, sacrifice, altar and priesthood; the connection is the stated deprivation, without equating the passages' dates.

Azariah asks that a crushed soul and humbled spirit be accepted as with burnt offerings. The psalm likewise contrasts burnt offerings with the broken spirit and humbled heart that God does not despise, bringing inward humility into the language of acceptable sacrifice.

The prayer's explicit trust clause affirms that those who trust God will not be put to shame. The psalm similarly joins trust in God with freedom from shame. This connection does not interpret the source's separate quoted 'behind Thee' phrases.
The companions turn to God with their whole heart and seek His face. Deuteronomy describes seeking God with the whole heart in distress among the nations and finding His covenant mercy.
The plea asks God to act with gentleness and mercy toward the shamed petitioners. Daniel's later prayer expressly rests its supplication on God's mercy rather than the petitioners' righteous deeds.
Azariah asks for rescue and glory for God's name. The psalm likewise asks the Savior to rescue and forgive for the glory of His name, joining deliverance with the honor of that name.
The prayer asks for the shame and humiliation of those who harm God's servants. The psalm likewise asks for the enemies' faces to be dishonored and for them to be ashamed and troubled.

relationship: recognition of the Lord's universal supremacy
rationale: The prayer asks that the opponents know that Thou alone art Lord and glorious over the inhabited world. The psalm similarly asks that they know the Lord alone is Most High over all the earth.
The description of the furnace's fuel and sevenfold heat returns to the king's command that it be heated seven times beyond what it needed to be heated.

The expanded account again describes the fire burning the Chaldeans around the furnace, recalling the earlier report that the flame killed the men who bound the companions while the companions were preserved.
The narrator says the Lord's angel entered with the three men. The king later sees a fourth figure with them and describes that figure as having the likeness of an angel of God.

The furnace's interior becomes like a dew-laden breeze, and the fire does not injure the men. Hebrews includes extinguishing the power of fire among the works of faith; this recalls the deliverance motif without explicitly naming the men here.
The three men begin their hymn together in one voice. Within that hymn Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael are explicitly summoned to bless God because He rescued them from the fire.
The hymn blesses the God of the fathers and His enduring glory. David's blessing likewise addresses the Lord, God of Israel and Father, from everlasting to everlasting.
The hymn blesses God in His holy temple. The psalm likewise locates the speaking of glory in His temple, joining the sanctuary with communal praise.
The hymn blesses God upon the throne of His kingdom. The psalm declares that the Lord has prepared His throne in heaven and that His kingdom rules over all.
The hymn addresses God as seated upon the cherubim. The psalm uses the same throne description when asking the shepherd of Israel to appear.
The hymn blesses God in heaven's firmament; the psalm expressly commands praise of Him in the firmament of His power.

relationship: shared summons to all God's works
rationale: All the Lord's works are called to bless Him. The psalm similarly calls all His works, in every place of His dominion, to bless the Lord.
The hymn summons the Lord's angels to bless Him; the psalm summons all His angels to praise Him. The same heavenly company receives the call to worship.
The heavens are summoned to bless the Lord. The psalm likewise summons the heavens of heavens to praise Him, giving the heavenly realm a voice in the creation hymn.
Both passages single out the waters above the heavens among those called to praise or bless the Lord, preserving that particular image of creation.
The hymn calls the Lord's powers to bless Him. The psalm similarly calls all His powers and ministers who do His will to bless the Lord.
Sun and moon are addressed together as worshippers of the Lord in both hymns; the shared pair gives the connection its specific content.
The stars of heaven are called to bless the Lord; the psalm likewise calls all the stars and light to praise Him.

relationship: praise of God's provision through rain
rationale: The hymn summons rain and dew to bless the Lord. The psalm calls for thanksgiving to God who covers heaven with clouds and prepares rain for the earth, relating rainfall to His praise.
The winds are called to bless the Lord. The psalm includes storm wind among the created forces fulfilling His word within its summons to praise.
Fire and heat are summoned to bless God even within the furnace song. The psalm also includes fire among the created forces that fulfill His word and praise Him.
The hymn calls chill and cold to bless God. The psalm attributes ice and cold to Him, asks who can withstand His cold, and says His word melts the ice, placing these conditions under His authority.

relationship: praise of the maker of snow
rationale: The hymn includes snow with dew in its summons to bless God. The psalm praises God's giving of snow and ice and His word that melts them; snow is the particular shared element.

relationship: divine authority over ice and cold
rationale: Ice and cold are summoned to bless the Lord; the psalm names both as God's works and describes the ice melting at His word.
The hymn addresses hoarfrost and snow. The psalm likewise places snow and ice within creation's praise, describing these wintry elements as fulfilling God's word.
The hymn summons nights and days to bless the Lord; the psalm explicitly declares that both day and night belong to Him. Both retain the paired ordering of time under God.
Light and darkness are called to bless God. Genesis describes God bringing light into being, distinguishing it from darkness and naming the two; the hymn addresses that ordered pair within creation.

relationship: praise of the maker of clouds and lightning
rationale: Lightning and clouds are addressed in the hymn. The psalm likewise attributes the rising of clouds and the making of lightning for rain to the Lord, naming the same atmospheric works.
The earth is called to bless the Lord. The psalm likewise commands praise of the Lord from the earth before enumerating its creatures and forces.
Both hymns summon mountains and hills together into the praise of God, retaining the same paired features of the land.

The hymn addresses growing plants of the earth; the psalm specifically includes fruit-bearing trees and cedars among creation's worshippers. Those named trees belong to the plant life addressed by the hymn.

relationship: praise of God's provision through springs
rationale: Springs are summoned to bless the Lord. The psalm describes His sending springs into ravines to supply the animals' thirst, identifying their place in His care of creation.
The hymn addresses seas and rivers together. The psalm similarly calls the sea to be stirred and rivers to clap their hands, personifying these waters in joyful response to God.

relationship: liturgical parallel of creatures and depths
rationale: The hymn calls sea monsters and creatures moving in water to bless God. The psalm's corresponding summons names dragons and the deeps, bringing great creatures and deep waters into creation's praise.
The hymn calls the birds of heaven to bless the Lord; the psalm includes winged birds among the creatures called to praise Him.
Quadrupeds and wild animals are addressed together in the hymn. The psalm likewise calls wild animals and specifically cattle into creation's praise, overlapping the hymn's stated land-animal groups.
The hymn calls humankind to bless God. The psalm expands that human company into peoples, rulers, men, women, old and young, all summoned to praise the Lord.
Israel is explicitly called to bless the Lord in the hymn; the psalm issues the same call to the house of Israel.

The hymn summons the Lord's priests to bless Him; the psalm calls the house of Aaron to bless Him. Exodus 28:1 explicitly appoints Aaron and his sons to priestly service, establishing the priestly household addressed by the psalm.
The hymn calls the Lord's servants to bless Him. The psalm likewise addresses all the Lord's slaves standing in His house and commands them to bless Him.

relationship: shared description of the worshipping company
rationale: The hymn includes the spirits and souls of righteous people among those blessing God. Hebrews describes the heavenly assembly as including the spirits of righteous ones made perfect, alongside angels and the assembly before God.
The hymn summons holy people and the humble in heart to bless God. The psalm likewise calls the meek to hear and rejoice and invites them to magnify the Lord together.
The named companions thank God for rescue from death and the furnace. Their earlier answer had trusted His rescue and maintained their refusal to worship the king's idol.
Both passages call for thanksgiving to the Lord because He is good or kind and His mercy is forever, joining the summons with the same enduring-mercy refrain.
Both passages call for thanks to the God of gods and give His everlasting mercy as the refrain. The divine title and the reason for thanksgiving correspond.

relationship: same-chapter audible hymn and royal response
rationale: The king hears the men singing and sees them alive. The earlier account identified the three men beginning their hymn in one voice, supplying the singing to which he reacts.
The king sees four unharmed, unbound figures and describes the fourth as angelic. The narrator has already described the Lord's angel joining the three and the furnace becoming harmless to them.
The king now calls the three men out of the fire as servants of the Most High. Earlier he had ordered those same men bound and thrown into it; his new command reverses their confinement.

relationship: shared promise and narrative of preservation in fire
rationale: The inspection finds no burning of the men's bodies or hair and no fire damage to their clothing. Isaiah's assurance to Israel describes passing through fire without being burned up, sharing the particular motif of preservation in fire narrated here.

relationship: same-chapter confession confirming the companions' answer
rationale: The king credits their God and His angel with rescue and recalls their refusal to worship another god. Both rescue and exclusive allegiance were expressed in the companions' earlier answer to him.
The king now declares that no other god can rescue in this way. This answers his earlier challenge asking what god could rescue the companions from his hands.

The king grants the three companions authority over the country after their rescue. Earlier Daniel had petitioned for them to be appointed over Babylonia's affairs; the passages trace his request and their subsequent royal service without equating the precise rank of each notice.

Both accounts explicitly introduce an episode in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year: the image's construction and the king's account of prosperity before his dream. The shared dating is retained without adding an order of events within that year.
Nebuchadnezzar again experiences a troubling dream that disturbs his peace. The earlier court narrative similarly begins with his dream and disturbed sleep before Daniel supplies its interpretation.
The great tree seen growing upon the earth is expressly identified in the interpretation as the king. The target supplies the image's stated referent.
The tree reaches heaven and the clouds. Daniel interprets that exalted height as the king's elevation above people and the pride of his heart against the Holy One.
Birds nest in the tree whose branches shelter and sustain living creatures. The interpretation identifies its nesting birds with the peoples, languages and countries serving the king.
An angel is sent in strength from heaven. The interpretation explicitly recalls the angel's mission and the tree's cutting down as the great God's judgment upon the king.
The Most High commands the tree's removal and destruction. Daniel explains that command as divine judgment against the king, followed by custody and removal to a deserted place.
The instruction leaves one root in the earth. Daniel expressly explains the root's preservation as the keeping of the king's throne for him for a time.
The vision assigns seven years of changed bodily existence and grazing. Nebuchadnezzar later reports seven years bound and fed grass like an ox, recounting that announced humiliation.

The judgment is to teach the king the heavenly Lord's authority over all things. His later thanksgiving credits God with creation, changing times and transferring kingdoms, expressing the lesson in his own royal confession.

The vision describes the fallen figure eating grass and being held in bonds. Nebuchadnezzar later reports being bound and fed grass like an ox for seven years, corresponding to those particular conditions.
Daniel is summoned as chief of the learned experts and interpreter of dreams. The earlier narrative records his appointment as ruler and leader of Babylon's learned men after the first royal dream.
Daniel's astonishment and changed appearance accompany the interpretation of the king's dream. At the end of his own beast vision, he again reports overwhelming astonishment and a changed condition.
Daniel identifies the king as the great tree planted in the earth, explicitly returning to the image first described in the dream.
The peoples and countries serving the king explain the birds nesting in the great tree, whose branches and fruit shelter and sustain living creatures in the dream.
The interpretation repeats the tree's reaching heaven and the clouds and explains it through the king's elevation and proud heart. The height of the image receives its explicit royal meaning.

Daniel connects the king's destruction of God's house with the consecrated people's sins. Chronicles similarly narrates the people's desecration and rejection of God's messengers before the Chaldean assault burns the Lord's house.
The interpretation explicitly recalls the angel sent in strength and the command to cut down the tree, identifying that action as divine judgment against the king.

The explanation describes the Most High and His angels rushing against the king. The dream had portrayed an angel sent from heaven announcing the Most High's command against the tree representing him.
The interpretation predicts the king's custody. He later describes himself as bound for seven years and fed grass, reporting the announced loss of royal freedom.
The surviving root means the king's throne is kept for him. The later restoration of his kingdom and glory records the outcome corresponding to that assurance.

Daniel advises the king to redeem his injustices by almsgiving while seeking mercy. Sirach expressly compares almsgiving's atonement for sins with water extinguishing fire, joining the same act with the treatment of sin.

Nebuchadnezzar keeps the vision's judgment in his heart after hearing it. Daniel later says he fixed the matter of his own vision in his heart; both accounts conclude the hearing of a troubling revelation with inward retention.

relationship: narrative illustration of a wisdom warning
rationale: The king boasts of Babylon as the product of his might and glory immediately before judgment removes his authority. Proverbs warns that insolence precedes ruin and commends humility instead, matching the movement from royal self-exaltation to downfall.
The heavenly sentence transfers Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom and says God gives kingship to whomever He wishes. Daniel's earlier praise had expressly described God transferring and appointing kings.
The sentence announces seven years of humiliation, grass as food and bonds in place of glory. The king's subsequent account reports seven years bound and fed grass like an ox.

The heavenly voice announces that the sentence will be fulfilled without failure. The king's following account reports the bonds, grass diet and seven-year period that the preceding sentence had specified.
Nebuchadnezzar reports the seven years of bonds and grass as food. The earlier heavenly sentence had named those same conditions in place of his royal glory.

The king describes altered flesh and heart, animal-like hair and nails, and life among wild animals. The vision had announced bodily change and grazing with animals for seven years; the connection concerns that changed existence.

relationship: same-chapter restoration promised by the root
rationale: The angel announces the restoration of kingship after the seven years. Daniel's earlier explanation of the preserved root had said that the place of the king's throne would be kept for him.
The return of kingdom and glory fulfills the interpretation that the unuprooted root represented the preservation of the king's throne.
The restored king praises God for changing seasons and times and replacing kings. Daniel's earlier thanksgiving had used those same actions to confess God's authority over time and royal power.

relationship: exclusive divine power over life and death
rationale: Nebuchadnezzar contrasts the powerless national gods with the God of heaven, who can kill and make alive. Deuteronomy likewise joins God's uniqueness with His power to put to death and make alive.

The king's circular letter thanks God for returning his throne, authority and greatness. The preceding narrative had reported the restoration of his kingdom and glory, which the letter now proclaims publicly.

Nebuchadnezzar addresses all nations and countries about God's wonders and enduring authority. Darius later writes to nations, countries and languages, calling them to worship the enduring God who rescued Daniel. Both are royal proclamations of God's action.

The preface anticipates fingers writing on the plaster wall opposite the lamp during Baltasar's banquet. The narrative reports that same writing scene in its own sequence; the preface's additional details are retained rather than merged into the verse.

The preface gives the written terms with glosses concerning numbering, removal and weighing. Daniel's later interpretation applies the message to the numbered end of the kingship and transfer to the Medes and Persians; the differing wording and order are preserved.

relationship: provenance and later misuse of sacred vessels
rationale: The vessels requested for Baltasar's drinking are identified as those Nebuchadnezzar brought from God's house in Jerusalem. The opening exile narrative records that removal of sacred vessels to Babylon.
The guests drink from the brought-in vessels. Daniel's later accusation specifically recalls the drinking from the living God's temple vessels and their accompanying praise of idols.

relationship: living Creator contrasted with human-made images
rationale: Baltasar's company blesses handmade idols while failing to honor the God who holds their breath. Acts likewise says God gives life and breath and rejects thinking of deity as gold, silver or stone shaped by human art.
The hand writing on the plaster opposite the light corresponds to the writing scene already summarized in the native preface, which also gives the message and its glosses.

The king promises purple clothing, a gold necklace and authority over a third part of the kingdom. The later verse reports all three rewards conferred on Daniel, preserving the stated portion of the kingdom.

relationship: failed court interpretation and divine revelation
rationale: The court's specialists cannot report the writing's interpretation. Daniel's earlier address had likewise distinguished what such specialists cannot disclose from the mysteries revealed by God in heaven.

The queen recalls Daniel from Judean captivity when the king needs an interpreter. Pharaoh's cupbearer likewise recalls a captive Hebrew whose earlier interpretations proved reliable, bringing an overlooked interpreter to royal attention.
The queen describes Daniel as surpassing Babylon's wise men. The earlier royal examination had already found Daniel and his companions far superior to the king's learned experts.
The queen recalls Daniel's extraordinary interpretations for Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar's own account describes summoning Daniel and receiving the entire interpretation of his dream.

The offer of purple clothing, a gold necklace and authority over a third part of the kingdom is later fulfilled in the king's grant to Daniel. The text specifies a portion of the kingdom, not a third-place rank.

relationship: same-chapter comparison of the written message
rationale: Daniel's reported reading gives numbering, reckoning and removal. The preface separately gives Mane, Phares and Thekel with its own glosses and order; these are related presentations of the wall's message, with their native differences retained.
Daniel's accusation recounts the temple vessels, drinking, praise of handmade idols and failure to bless the living God. Those are the particular acts already narrated at the banquet.

relationship: life and breath received from God
rationale: Daniel says the king's breath is in God's hand while rebuking praise of human-made idols. Acts likewise describes God as giver of life and breath and rejects identifying the divine with images formed by human art.

Daniel interprets the message as the end of the kingship and its transfer to the Medes and Persians. The final narrative says the interpretation came upon Baltasar and that the kingdom was transferred to those peoples.
The purple garment, gold necklace and authority over a third part of the kingdom fulfill the specific rewards promised to the one who could explain the writing.

The taking of kingship from the Chaldeans and its transfer to the Medes and Persians enacts the interpretation Daniel gave. This source unit reports the transfer without adding a statement that the king died that night.

The one hundred twenty-seven satraps introduced over the kingdom recur in the description of Daniel's proposed authority with the two other leaders. The target resumes the same stated administrative structure.

Daniel is one of three leaders over the satraps. The subsequent account describes the two men appointed with him and their plot when the whole-kingdom appointment is proposed, linking the three-person arrangement to the rivalry.

Daniel's wisdom, knowledge and holy spirit explain his distinction before Darius. The queen had earlier described him with the same combination of exceptional wisdom and a holy spirit when recommending him as an interpreter.

The plotters can find no sin or ignorant fault in Daniel to accuse before the king. Daniel later asserts that neither ignorant fault nor sin was found in him and that the king listened to misleading accusers.

The restriction is designed to exploit Daniel's known habit of praying three times daily. After learning of it, he continues the same practice toward Jerusalem, showing that the plot targets his established worship.

relationship: same-chapter reversal of a worship decree
rationale: The proposed decree permits requests only to Darius and threatens prayer to any god. Darius's later proclamation commands the people of his kingdom to worship Daniel's God, reversing the earlier direction of royal religious policy.

The conspirators seek an unalterable restriction because they know Daniel's three daily prayers. Their later surveillance catches him doing precisely that, carrying out the stated plan against his worship.

Darius establishes the restriction. When the accusers later repeat its thirty-day terms and penalty, he confirms that their statement is exact and that the restriction remains, reaffirming the order he ratified.

Daniel prays with his windows open toward Jerusalem while living under foreign rule. Solomon's prayer anticipates captives praying toward their land, the chosen city and the temple, giving that direction of prayer a stated covenant setting.
The men catch Daniel praying three times each day, the very practice they had named when arranging the restriction to bring him down.

relationship: same-chapter decree quoted back to the king
rationale: The accusers repeat the thirty-day prohibition on prayer to any god except Darius and its lions-pit penalty. Those are the terms previously proposed to the king.

The men invoke the decrees of the Medes and Persians while demanding that this command not be altered. Esther states that a writing issued at the king's command and sealed with his ring cannot be contradicted. These are related appeals to royal authorization, with the distinct formulations and rulers preserved.

relationship: same-chapter accusation checked against the narrated act
rationale: The report accuses Daniel of seeking his God three times daily. The earlier account has already described his three daily supplications toward Jerusalem after learning of the restriction.

Darius grieves yet orders Daniel into the lions' pit under pressure from the officials. In the other narrative, a king faced with a crowd gathered against him hands Daniel over to destruction. The royal surrender under pressure is compared without equating the episodes.

relationship: same-chapter human inability and divine rescue
rationale: The king cannot rescue Daniel from the officials. He then assures Daniel that his God will rescue him, and the narrative reports God shutting the lions' mouths, contrasting royal inability with divine protection.

Darius assures Daniel that his God will rescue him from the lions and tells him to take courage until morning. The night account then reports God caring for Daniel and shutting the lions' mouths so that they do not trouble him.

relationship: parallel sealing of a stone entrance
rationale: A stone closes Daniel's pit and receives royal seals to prevent his removal. Matthew likewise records a stone sealed at the tomb with a guard; Matthew 27:64 states the aim of preventing removal of the body. The connection is the physical security measure, not an assertion that the events are identical.

God shuts the lions' mouths so that they do not harm Daniel. Hebrews lists shutting lions' mouths among the works of faith, recalling the same distinctive deliverance motif without explicitly naming Daniel in that verse.

Darius comes to the pit after Daniel's confinement. The other narrative likewise has the mourning king visit the pit and see Daniel alive; this compares the royal visit without making the separate episodes one event.
The king asks whether Daniel's God has saved him from the lions. The question returns to his earlier assurance of rescue and his accompanying instruction to take courage until morning.
Daniel's declaration that he is still alive supplies the first direct answer to the king's earlier assurance that Daniel's God would rescue him from the lions.

Daniel says no ignorant fault or sin was found in him before the king. The earlier account independently states that the plotters could find no such fault, supporting the specific claim of innocence in his answer.

The assembled forces see that the lions have not troubled Daniel. The night account had attributed that unharmed state to God shutting the lions' mouths; the later gathering confirms the outcome publicly.

Daniel's accusers are thrown to the lions and killed after he is preserved. The other narrative likewise casts those responsible for his destruction into the pit, where they are devoured. Daniel 6 additionally names wives and children; the comparison does not add them to the other account.

Darius writes to all nations, countries and languages after Daniel's rescue. Nebuchadnezzar's earlier circular letter likewise addresses all peoples and countries to proclaim what God has done, framing a royal acknowledgment of divine power.

relationship: parallel confession of enduring divine rule
rationale: Darius's proclamation calls people to worship the God who lives and endures from generation to generation. Nebuchadnezzar's letter likewise proclaims everlasting divine kingship and authority from generation to generation.

relationship: human-made idols contrasted with divine rescue
rationale: Darius contrasts the inability of handmade idols to save with God's rescue of Daniel. The psalm depicts the nations' metal idols as human-made and without breath or functioning senses, exposing the powerlessness of what their makers trust.

The closing notice records Cyrus receiving the kingdom after Darius. The earlier notice that Daniel remained until Cyrus's first year supplies the corresponding royal setting for the continuation of Daniel's service.
